chief_complaint: inability to retract prepuce/foreskin over glans penis
hpi_details: A 56-year-old male presents to the clinic with inability to retract the foreskin over the glans penis. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening.
ideas: thinks it might be related to phimosis
concerns: worried about potential complications and long term recovery
expectations: wants complete diagnostic evaluation and treatment plan

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Phimosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Assess for infection, diabetes, lichen sclerosus, and suspicious penile lesions; gentle topical steroid therapy may be appropriate for uncomplicated phimosis, while persistent pathologic phimosis or suspected malignancy warrants urology review.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: inability to retract prepuce/foreskin over glans penis

Key HPI features: A 56-year-old male presents to the clinic with inability to retract the foreskin over the glans penis. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Phimosis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Phimosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Forcing back a tight foreskin, which can cause paraphimosis.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Forcing retraction, missing paraphimosis or urinary retention, or overlooking an ulcerated, bleeding, or indurated penile lesion.
management_principles: Avoid forceful retraction; treat confirmed uncomplicated phimosis with clinician-directed topical steroid and gentle stretching, and refer persistent, scarred, or suspicious cases for urology assessment and possible circumcision.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of inability to retract prepuce/foreskin over glans penis. HPI: phimosis.
reference_soap.objective: Inspect the foreskin and glans for inflammation, scarring, lichen sclerosus, or a suspicious lesion; assess urinary stream and screen for diabetes or recurrent infection as indicated.
reference_soap.assessment: Phimosis; exclude balanitis, lichen sclerosus, paraphimosis, urinary obstruction, and penile malignancy in an adult with new or progressive narrowing.
reference_soap.plan: Avoid forceful retraction. If uncomplicated, consider a time-limited topical steroid with gentle stretching under clinical guidance; arrange urology review for persistent scarring, recurrent infection, suspicious lesions, or consideration of circumcision. Seek emergency care for paraphimosis or inability to pass urine.

Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Phimosis

teaching.one_liner: Urology evaluation for patient presenting with inability to retract prepuce/foreskin over glans penis.
red_flags: Paraphimosis with a swollen, painful glans

must_ask.objective: Onset and severity of foreskin tightness
must_ask.say: When did you first notice that your foreskin was difficult to retract, and has it become tighter?
Do you have pain, redness, swelling, itching, or discharge around the head of the penis?
Have you had burning when you urinate, a weak stream, or any difficulty passing urine?
Has the foreskin ever become stuck behind the head of the penis or caused severe swelling?
Do you have diabetes, recurrent genital infections, or a history of skin conditions such as lichen sclerosus?
